1:
Why the apostle does not abolish the institution is the question. Ellicott answers at length: slavery was perhaps the most perplexing question Christianity had to face, entering all grades and ranks, so that the fabric of society seemed knit together by it; to preach against it as hateful to God would have been to preach revolution in its most violent form. Christ and his disciples therefore left society as they found it, uprooting no ancient landmarks, trusting by a new and lovely example slowly to raise men higher; and he thinks the result has not disappointed them, since this curse at least is disappearing fast. Henry states the principle drily: if Christianity finds servants under the yoke it continues them under it, for the gospel does not cancel obligations men lie under by the law of nature or by consent. Clarke puts it as a rule — civil rights are never abolished by any communications from God’s Spirit.

Calvin explains why the charge was needed. At the beginning of the gospel slaves cheered their hearts as if the signal had been given for their emancipation, and Paul labours in all his writings to repress that desire; for it is customary to seize, for the advantage of the flesh, everything that has the slightest appearance of being in our favour. Told they were all brethren, they concluded it unreasonable that they should be the slaves of brethren. Calvin then widens it past slavery: owing to the false opinion of his own excellence which every person entertains, no one patiently endures that others should rule over him, and they who cannot avoid it obey reluctantly while inwardly they fret and rage. The apostle cuts off such disputes with a single word, requiring that those under the yoke submit willingly and not inquire whether they deserve that lot or a better.

The reason given is reputation. Robertson supposes the danger concretely — the heathen might say Christian slaves were less dependable than others — and adds a philological note that lands hard: the word for masters is the strict correlative of slave, and is the word from which our despot comes, where the other word for lord has a wider outlook. That, he says, is always where the shoe pinches. Gill notes that the false teachers had argued servitude was inconsistent with Christian liberty.

On believing masters they divide over how far the brotherhood reaches. Barnes is the most guarded. Paul supposed a man might own slaves and be converted, since God may convert men pursuing any wickedness; but how long he might hold his fellow men in bondage and yet be a Christian is quite another question, and there is no intimation that the apostle thought it right to persevere, nor that such a man was entitled to all the respect due to the Christian name. Wesley knows the difficulty from experience: those who live in a religious community know that greater grace is needed to bear a brother’s faults than an unbeliever’s.

The last clause is obscure, and Clarke lays out the options: that those who profit by the slaves’ service are the faithful and beloved, or that the servants partake of benefits from Christian masters, or that the benefit is the grace of the gospel — which he rejects, since the word is nowhere used of the gospel — and he records a manuscript reading godliness instead. Ellicott takes the first and makes it a motto for the Christian slave: every good piece of work I do will be a kindness shown to one who loves my Lord. Chrysostom, coming to the charge that follows, makes it a lesson for teachers: a teacher has need not only of authority but of gentleness, and not only of gentleness but of authority; for if physicians entreat the sick in order to relieve their sickness, much more should we entreat those we teach.
3:
Who these teachers were is reconstructed from the denunciation itself. Clarke names them religious levellers, who preached that the converted servant had as much right to the master’s service as the master had to his, and adds that teachers of this kind have been in vogue long since the apostle’s day. Barnes states their argument before rejecting it — that God made all men equal, that all had been redeemed by the same blood, that all true Christians were fellow-heirs, and that it was wrong to hold a Christian brother in bondage — and objects that from undeniable principles they inferred that slaves should at once assert their freedom, producing insurrection instead of removing the evil by the silent influence of Christian principles. Gill widens the charge: these men despised dominion of every kind, civil, ecclesiastical and domestic.

What the wholesome words are they take differently. Clarke reads the adjective as healing, doctrines that give health to the soul, and insists the reference is to the general tenor of the gospel and not to anything our Lord said about slaves, since with political questions he scarcely ever meddled. Ellicott is bolder and names the sayings he thinks were meant: render unto Caesar, blessed are the meek, take up the cross daily, resist not evil, love your enemies — current watchwords in the churches, so that it was on the spirit of the Sermon on the Mount that the apostle grounded his advice to the slaves. Robertson notes the genitive can be taken either way, of a collection of sayings from the Lord or of doctrine about him.

The three words that follow are diagnosed like symptoms. Barnes explains that the verb rendered proud means to smoke or fume, then to be inflated; Clarke has him blown up, Ellicott blinded with pride, Robertson that ignorance is a frequent companion of conceit. The word for doting means to be sick, and Barnes makes the simile exact: such a man has no appetite for solid food but craves what gratifies a diseased one, desiring not sound doctrine but controversies bearing the same relation to it that a sick man’s fancies bear to substantial food.

Clarke will not leave that word alone, and his outburst is the strongest thing here. How little good have religious disputes ever done to mankind, or to the cause of truth! Most controversialists have succeeded only in souring their own tempers and irritating their opponents; truth seems rarely to be their object, for they labour to accredit their own party by defaming others, and from generals they descend to particulars, and then personal abuse is the order of the day. He asks whether such men should not be deemed disturbers of the public peace. Ellicott gives the same complaint a list, naming the words over which wild war has raged through the Christian ages — predestination, election, faith, inspiration, person, regeneration — and questions never to be solved on earth, which have rent whole churches and sown irreconcilable hatred.

The next phrase turns on a disputed reading. Barnes defends the received text: the word occurs nowhere else, meaning mis-employment or idle occupation, from a verb meaning to rub in pieces or wear away. The notion of contention is not necessarily in it; the sense is of employments that merely consumed time without advantage, so that idle employments would suit better than either rendering the translators gave. Robertson and Ellicott prefer the better-attested word: mutual irritations, or obstinate conflicts. On the last clause Ellicott insists the article settles it: the sense is not that gain is godliness but that godliness is a source of gain, by far the gravest of the charges. Wesley puts it where it hurts: thinking the best religion is the getting of money, a commoner case than is usually supposed. Clarke adds that the closing command to withdraw is wanting in many authorities and probably spurious.
6:
Ellicott hears the turn as a swerve, an admirable instance of what has been called going off at a word: the hateful word gain, just used of the false teachers, suggests a danger to which many in a congregation drawn from a wealthy commercial city were hourly exposed. The reasoning, he supposes, was that these men expect godliness to be turned into gain — and though terribly mistaken, there is a sense in which their miserable notion is true. Henry makes the point as an epigram: though Christianity is the worst trade, it is the best calling in the world; those who make a trade of it to serve their turn find it a sorry trade, but those who mind it as their calling find it a gainful one.

The second noun divides them. Barnes takes it as a state of mind, a calm and satisfied feeling free from murmuring; the Greek means properly self-sufficiency, used here in a good sense of a mind satisfied with its lot, and he cites an older English version reading, godliness is great riches if a man be content with that he hath. Clarke takes it as a competency, that measure of secular things necessary for the support of life, and guards it at once: not what this or the other person may deem a competency, but food, raiment and lodging. Henry reports both readings without choosing, observing that wherever there is true godliness there will be contentment. Robertson notes that this attitude of mind is the apostle’s conception of great gain; Wesley calls contentment the inseparable companion of true religion.

The argument from birth and death they treat as self-evident and then decorate. Barnes says nothing is more obvious: our coming into the world introduces no property to what the race already possessed, and our going removes none we may have helped it accumulate. Clarke produces two sentences from a Roman moralist contemporary with the apostle which are almost word for word the same: no man is born rich, and every one who comes into the world is commanded to be content with food and raiment; and nature shakes off all encumbrances at our going as at our coming, so that you cannot carry back more than you brought in. Ellicott notes that the sentence is quoted in a letter written early in the second century, which shows the epistle was known and treasured that early. Gill turns it into comfort under stripping providences: we came in naked, and whatever we have is more than we brought. Wesley turns it into a prayer: to what purpose then do we heap together so many things? give me one thing, a safe and ready passage to my own country.

What the last verse permits is the real question. Clarke and Wesley take the second to mean covering in general, house and lodging as well as clothing, and Wesley draws the strict conclusion: this is all a Christian needs, and all his religion allows him to desire. Barnes will not go so far. Food and raiment stand for our necessities in general, the whole named by a part, and we cannot suppose the apostle forbids a comfortable habitation, or the means of knowledge, or conveniences for the worship of God; the point is only that having what meets our necessities we should not make wealth the object of anxious pursuit. Ellicott guards it from the other side, against the false asceticism the same letter attacks earlier: this teaching neither rejects nor deems evil the fair things of life, but never covets them. It was one thing to be rich and another to wish to be rich; a man might be rich without sin, but the longing for wealth at once exposed him to grave danger. Robertson notes both nouns are plurals, nourishments and coverings, each occurring nowhere else in the New Testament.
9:
They all insist the warning is not aimed at the rich. Gill says so first: some rich men are good men and do much good with their riches, and are as free from these snares as any; the apostle points not at rich men but at those determined to be rich, whether they ever attain it or not. Barnes finds the point in the verb, which is not the sign of the future tense but a word for actual purpose, and adds a shrewd aside: perhaps nothing more would be needed to make a poor man satisfied with his lot than acquaintance with the cares of a rich one. Ellicott guards the other side, lest the words be taken by some unpractical school of asceticism to mean that voluntary poverty is peculiarly pleasing to God — the strange mistake, he says, on which the mendicant orders were founded. Robertson defines it as a will to be rich at any cost and in haste.

Clarke is the exception, and hardest. Those meant get all they can, save all they can, and keep all they get, apprehending no danger because they seek riches honestly; and by rich, he thinks, the apostle refers back to food and raiment, so that whoever has more than these is rich in the sense meant here.

The snare is worked out carefully. Clarke gives the word a sharper sense — a pit dug in the ground, filled with sharp stakes and slightly covered, so that whoever steps on it tumbles in and is pierced through — and so ties the trap of this verse to the piercing of the next. Ellicott calls it a very tangle of conflicting motives, each gratification of the ruling passion excused under the plausible names of industry, home claims, healthy enterprise. He then turns it on the reader: we pray so often, lead us not into temptation, and in the same hour, perhaps with the same breath, we long for our means to be increased.

On the famous sentence they divide three ways. Clarke would translate it of all these evils, those just enumerated, since the love of money certainly was not the root of the first transgression; and he protests at the misquotation — how often do we hear that Scripture says money is the root of all evil, when it says no such thing. Barnes agrees it is not literally true, since the evils of ambition and intemperance and the hatred of God cannot be traced to it, and takes the words as a popular saying; but he keeps the same distinction, that the apostle does not call money an evil at all, only the love of it. Ellicott defends the strong rendering against those who soften it to a root, arguing that the article properly disappears before the predicate, and glosses it: not that every evil must come from covetousness, but that there is no conceivable evil which may not spring from it. Robertson reports the sentence is a proverb attributed to two ancient philosophers, in whose form the word for a mother city stands where root stands here, and remarks that men today need no proof that they will commit any sin for money.

Gill locates the sin precisely: not money, which is God’s creature and serves good purposes, nor every love of it, since some desire is required by the duties we owe to God and men; but an immoderate and insatiable love, properly idolatry, when a man loves it not only besides but above God. On the last clause Ellicott hears the psalm which says their sorrows shall be multiplied that hasten after another god, and takes the many sorrows to be the gnawings of conscience; Wesley names them a guilty conscience, tormenting passions, and desires contrary to reason and to one another, and ends where the verse does: how cruel are worldly men to themselves.
11:
The title is old, and they trace it. Gill takes it from the Old Testament, where Elijah and Elisha are so called, and applies it to a peculiar office; Wesley makes it a prophet, a messenger of God, or a man of another world; Robertson notes it occurs only twice in the New Testament, general there and personal here. Ellicott builds a reading on the personal address, and begins by warning himself. A commentator speaks with caution when he approaches a direct personal reference, for we have so long surrounded these writers with a halo of reverence that we forget they were men tempted like ours; we lose something of the reality of the apostolic story when in the saint we forget the man. His conclusion is that the old apostle dreaded for his young disciple the corrupting danger of the wealth of the city where he held so great a charge.

Clarke says it without the preamble and more sharply. Escape for thy life — even thou art not out of reach of the love of money. How many ministers of religion have been ruined by this, and how much has religion itself suffered by it! Robertson agrees the preacher cannot afford to parley with such temptations, and notes both verbs are vivid present imperatives. Wesley says flee as from a serpent. Henry puts the difficulty at the other end: it ill becomes any men, especially men of God, to set their hearts on this world — but who can give such a charge who is not himself above the love of what wealth can buy?

The metaphor of the second verse is agreed and enjoyed. Barnes refers it to the Grecian games: seize eternal life as eagerly as the competitors laid hold on the prize. Clarke renders the phrase agonize the good agony and keeps the allusion running: Timothy has been called into this arena, accepted as fit to enter the lists, has taken the engagements upon him before many witnesses, and many eyes are on him to see whether he fights manfully. Ellicott calls it the metaphor the apostle loved so well, and defines the good fight as the contest against the world, the flesh and the devil — good partly because waged on behalf of the faith, but still more because from faith it draws its strength. Robertson glosses the second imperative as, get a grip on.

Barnes turns the calling into a rebuke. God does not call his people that they may become rich, nor convert them that they may devote themselves to the business of gain; they are called to a higher work. Yet how many professing Christians live as if God had called them to the special business of making money, and pursue it with a zeal that would do honour to such a calling, if that had been his grand object in converting them.

When the good confession was made none can settle, and they offer four answers. Barnes thinks of the public profession made on embracing Christianity, or the solemn setting apart to the ministry, and adds that one of the best ways of reclaiming a backslider is to bring back the vows he then made. Wesley and Robertson name baptism, the public confession which many witnessed. Clarke argues for a persecution: it is said elsewhere that our brother Timothy is set at liberty, so he had been imprisoned for the testimony of Christ, and perhaps it was then, not at his ordination, that he made this confession — if not a martyr, he was a confessor. Ellicott finds that reading most probable in itself, and rejects it only for the difficulty of fitting so terrible an experience into a short life. Wesley leaves a sting: Timothy confessed before many witnesses, to which they all assented; his Master witnessed the good confession, but the governor did not assent to it.
13:
Why God is named as the giver of life here is the first question. Chrysostom answers that the oath increases the disciple’s awe and secures him, and that the attribute is chosen for comfort: here is consolation in the dangers awaiting him, and a remembrance of the resurrection — fear not death, since thou art the servant of God who can give life to all things. Barnes reaches the same conclusion less confidently: if obedience should cost Timothy his life, he was to remember that God had power to raise him up again. Ellicott prefers the older reading, who preserveth all things, bringing forward the Preserver rather than the Creator, so that Timothy fights mindful of one who could preserve him, on earth or in Paradise.

The example beside the charge is read alike by all. Chrysostom makes it the pattern: as the Master did, so ought we, for it was for this cause he witnessed, that we might tread in his steps. Henry observes that Christ died not only as a sacrifice but as a martyr, and points the application: his confession that his kingdom is not of this world should draw off all his followers from the love of this world. Robertson insists the preposition means in the presence of, not in the time of, notes the verb here is the one for bearing witness rather than for confessing, and infers the apostle knew some facts that appear in the fourth Gospel.

What is to be kept without spot divides them. Barnes finds it harsh to apply the epithet to a command, and thinks it may be construed of Timothy himself, that he keep the commandment so as to be without spot. Clarke wants both, and is emphatic about the first: let there be no blot on the sacred book, add nothing, take nothing, change nothing, but deliver down the truth as thou hast had it from God himself; then let nothing in thy conduct be contrary to it — keep the truth, and the truth will keep thee. Cyril of Jerusalem, quoting the charge in a catechetical lecture, makes it a deposit: faith is like putting money into the bank, and God requires the account, for a treasure of life has been committed to thee and the Master demands it at his appearing.

The clause about the appearing draws the best observation here from Ellicott. The speedy return was looked for in the church of the first days; but by slow degrees, as one great teacher after another fell asleep and the first generation passed away with no fresh sign given, the strong expressions of that first fervour began to be qualified, as in this letter written far on in the writer’s life. The impression is that he had given up hope of seeing that day himself, but thought his son in the faith probably would. He adds that the doxology was not improbably taken from a hymn loved by the Ephesian Christians and sung in their churches.

On the doxology they compete in precision. Gill distinguishes: angels are immortal, and the souls of men, and their bodies will be after the resurrection, but none have it of themselves — God only has it originally and underivatively. Barnes agrees; Clarke adds that all beings not eternal must be mutable, and that because God is infinite he is incomprehensible, and incomprehensible to the mind is consequently invisible to the eye. Robertson suggests emperor worship may lie behind the word alone, one emperor having demanded to be addressed in these very terms. Ellicott shows the old covenant teaching the same by its symbols — the guarded bounds of Sinai, the veiled darkness of the holy of holies — and observes the Greek excludes all created beings, not men only. Wesley makes one qualification: no man can see him with bodily eyes, yet we shall see him as he is.
17:
The turn from the earlier warning is deliberate. Ellicott marks it. The wish to be rich was a sure root of evil, but being rich is a very different thing; this class is surrounded with special perils, yet even as rich they may serve God faithfully, so the charge is not to strip themselves of their wealth but to use it wisely. Gill notes that Ephesus was a rich city and some rich men in it were called by grace; Ellicott presses the phrase in this world, since the Greek means an age, so that these riches are always terminable with life, and possibly sooner.

Against pride Barnes argues from what money cannot do. Property makes no distinction in the great things that pertain to character and salvation; it does not make a man wise, or learned, or great, or good, and in all these the man without wealth may be the superior. Let him reflect that his property is God’s gift, that it only increases his responsibility, and that it must all soon be left, and he be as poor as the beggar at his gate. Wesley says it harder: rich in such beggarly riches as this world affords, and not to think better of themselves for their money or anything it can purchase — O who regards this!

The uncertainty is illustrated, not argued. Barnes puts the cases: a man whose house is in flames, or who is shipwrecked, or whose child lies dying, or who is himself dying, can derive no advantage from being richer than other men. Robertson calls the phrase a vigorous oxymoron and sums it in four words, riches have wings; God alone is stable, not wealth. On the clause that follows Clarke turns generous: God gives not merely what is necessary but what renders life comfortable, so the comforts of life come from him as well as the necessaries — God gives liberally, man divides it badly. Henry adds the complaint that many have riches but enjoy them poorly, not having a heart to use them.

Doing good is then made the best enjoyment. Clarke calls relieving the wants of our fellow creatures the highest luxury a human being can enjoy on this side of the grave; Ellicott calls it the only enjoyment which never fails and never disappoints. On the two adjectives Ellicott distinguishes finely: the first points to the hand which generously gives, the second to the heart which lovingly sympathises — the one obeying the charge to give to him that asketh, the other the command to rejoice with those who rejoice. Clarke wants the giving governed by need rather than partiality, and not confined at home but scattered abroad; Wesley divides it otherwise, distributing singly to particular persons and communicating in public works of charity. Henry asks what the best estate is worth, more than as it gives opportunity of doing the more good.

The last verse produces the most interesting note here, from Clarke. He thinks the form of speech borrowed from an older Jewish book which bids a man give alms according to his abundance, treasuring up a good reward against the day of necessity; then he adopts Wesley’s own paraphrase by name: this treasure is an abundant reward by the free mercy of God, and cannot be earned by almsdeeds, though such deeds come up for a memorial before God. Gill points the contrast: what men lay up here is for others, for children or friends or strangers, they know not who — a wise man or a fool, or even an enemy. Robertson names the paradox, laying up in store by giving away, and reports the older authorities read not eternal life but that which is truly life; Ellicott takes the same reading and guards it, since such statements in no way weaken the truth that men are saved only by the blood of Christ.
20:
Ellicott hears a change of hand in the last two verses. The letter was dictated to a scribe, but, as seems to have been the apostle’s habit elsewhere, the closing reminder was added by his own hand, so that these words are the very handwriting of the worn and aged man; and with the vocative he writes no longer to a church or pastor, but to his own friend and pupil.

What the trust is they agree about, and Robertson names the figure: a banking term, common in the papyri, for something placed beside another as a deposit, with an aorist of urgency — keep the deposit. Gill calls it the Gospel, a rich treasure in earthen vessels, to be kept pure and faithfully dispensed, and adds that it may include the gifts for its ministration. Barnes says the honour of the gospel had been committed to Timothy, who was to guard it and not suffer it to be wrested from him.

Ellicott then quotes a fifth-century writer on what keeping a trust means, and the definition is the sharpest thing in the chapter. It is something entrusted to you to keep, not a possession you discovered; something received from another, not thought out for yourself; and of this trust you are nothing but the guardian. Gold have you received; see that you hand gold on to others. The same writer then puts the obvious objection — is there then to be no progress, no development, in religious teaching? — and answers that there should be real progress and marked development, but partaking of the nature of a progress and not of a change, as the members of the body grow stronger as the years roll on and yet always remain the same.

On the babblings they are brief. Barnes takes them as controversies which produce strife and do not edify; Ellicott observes that theological controversy seems to have been distasteful to the apostle, as tending to augment dissension and to exalt mere words into undue prominence; Wesley says it in six words — how weary of controversy was this acute disputant.

The last phrase has aged best, and Barnes handles it carefully. Religion has nothing to fear from true science, and the minister is not exhorted to dread it; real science in all its advances contributes to the support of religion, and in proportion as it is promoted will be found to sustain the Bible. Only false or pretended science need religion dread. Clarke reaches the same place by another road, following a commentator who takes the knowledge in question to be the inspired gift of understanding the older Scriptures: the false teachers pretended to it and dignified their misinterpretations with its name, and since by those interpretations they laboured to establish the Levitical atonements, their knowledge was rightly called oppositional, framed to establish doctrines subversive of the gospel. Clarke rejects the other proposal, that the Gnostics are in view, since it is not clear those heretics had any proper existence at this time. Wesley agrees that most of the ancient heretics were great pretenders to knowledge. Robertson notes the word for oppositions gives us antithesis and the word for falsely named gives us pseudonymous, both occurring only here.

The close draws three notes. Barnes says those who erred professed to be true Christians, were attracted by false philosophy, and so came to deny the doctrines of Christianity — a result not uncommon in the world. Ellicott reports the ancient authorities almost equally divided between the singular and the plural in the benediction, and accounts for the absence of the private greetings found in the second letter by the public nature of so much in this one. Clarke, surveying the subscriptions, finds them at odds, some naming Laodicea, one Athens, one Macedonia, one Nicopolis, and prefers Macedonia; Barnes cuts that short: these subscriptions, like the others, carry no authority.
